paths/great-schism-east-and-west/title: The Great Schism: East and West part ways
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/summary: The break between Rome and Constantinople was not a single event in 1054 but a slow estrangement over language, politics, papal authority and the creed, sealed by the Crusades and still being addressed today.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/0: Constantine founded Constantinople as a 'New Rome' (330). Over the following centuries the Greek-speaking East and Latin-speaking West grew apart in language, theology and politics, especially after the Western Empire fell in 476.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/1: Pope Leo I's Tome shaped the Christology of Chalcedon (451), but Leo rejected the council's canon 28, which gave Constantinople privileges second only to Rome because it was the imperial city. Rome grounded its primacy in Peter; the East tended to ground rank in a city's importance and conciliar consensus.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/2: The filioque enters the Western creed

The Spanish addition of 'and the Son' to the creed's article on the Spirit (Toledo, 589) spread through the Frankish church. The East objected both to the theology and to changing an ecumenical creed without an ecumenical council.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/3: Byzantine iconoclasm (from 726) and the restoration of icons at Nicaea II (787), defended by John of Damascus, were largely Eastern struggles; the Frankish court misunderstood the council's decisions, a sign of growing distance.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/4: When Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in Rome (800), Byzantium regarded it as usurpation. Carolingian theologians championed the filioque and criticised the Greeks.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/5: Photius and the mission to the Slavs

Rivalry over missions to the Slavs and Bulgarians, and the dispute between Patriarch Photius and Pope Nicholas I, produced a temporary schism (863-867). Photius' encyclical attacked the filioque. Meanwhile Cyril and Methodius' Slavonic liturgy and the baptism of Rus' (988) extended Byzantine Christianity northward.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/6: Papal legates led by Cardinal Humbert laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia; the patriarch's synod excommunicated the legates. Disputes included papal authority, the filioque and unleavened bread. At the time it looked like one more quarrel.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/7: Crusades and the sack of Constantinople

The Crusades brought Latins into the East in force. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople and installed a Latin patriarch; for many Orthodox this, more than 1054, made the schism real and bitter.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/8: Reunion councils at Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439) produced agreements signed under Byzantine political pressure but rejected by most Orthodox clergy and people (Mark of Ephesus refused to sign). The hesychast victory had meanwhile confirmed a distinct Eastern theology. Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453; later 'Eastern Catholic' churches united with Rome while keeping Eastern rites.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/steps/9: On 7 December 1965, at the close of Vatican II, Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the 1054 excommunications. Theological dialogue continues on primacy and the filioque, with recent popes (John Paul II, Francis) and patriarchs meeting regularly, though full communion has not been restored.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/quiz/0/: Filioque means 'and the Son', added to say the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/quiz/1/: Who were the principal figures in the excommunications of 1054?
Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius
Humbert, as papal legate, excommunicated Cerularius, who in turn anathematised the legates.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/quiz/2/: Which event do many Orthodox consider the real turning point that made the schism bitter?
The sack of Constantinople by the Fourth Crusade in 1204
The 1204 sack of Constantinople by Western crusaders left lasting bitterness.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/quiz/3/: Why did Pope Leo I reject canon 28 of Chalcedon?
It gave Constantinople privileges second only to Rome on political grounds
Leo held that Rome's primacy rested on Peter, not on imperial status, and rejected the canon.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/quiz/4/: What happened at the Council of Florence (1439)?
A lasting reunion of East and West
A union agreement that was largely rejected in the East
The union was signed under political pressure but rejected by most Orthodox; Mark of Ephesus refused to sign.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/quiz/5/: Paul VI and Athenagoras lifted them on 7 December 1965.
paths/great-schism-east-and-west/quiz/6/: Which council restored the veneration of icons in 787?
The Second Council of Nicaea, the seventh ecumenical council for both Orthodox and Catholics.
paths/christianity-beyond-the-west/title: Christianity beyond the West: Persia, Ethiopia, India, China
paths/christianity-beyond-the-west/summa: For its first thousand years Christianity was as much an Asian and African faith as a European one. Follow the churches of Armenia, Ethiopia, Persia, India and China, the councils that divided them, and their survival and renewal.
paths/christianity-beyond-the-west/steps: A multilingual beginning

Luke's Pentecost crowd included Parthians, Medes, Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Egypt and Libya (Acts 2:9-11). Christianity spread early in Syriac-speaking Edessa and Mesopotamia, outside the Roman Empire.
Armenia: the first Christian kingdom

According to tradition, Gregory the Illuminator converted King Tiridates III, making Armenia the first state to adopt Christianity (traditionally 301; some scholars prefer c. 314). Mesrop Mashtots later created the Armenian alphabet to translate the Bible.
Ethiopia: Frumentius at Aksum

Frumentius, a Syrian Christian captive who rose at the court of Aksum, was consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria; King Ezana adopted Christianity around 330-340. The Ethiopian church kept close ties with Alexandria for 1,600 years and preserved a distinctive canon and liturgy.
Syriac Christianity and Ephrem

Ephrem the Syrian, deacon of Nisibis and Edessa, wrote theology as poetry and hymns, showing a Semitic, non-Hellenistic way of doing theology that shaped both Syriac Orthodox and Church of the East traditions.
Persia and the Church of the East

Christians in the Persian Empire suffered persecution under Shapur II and organised their own synods (410). After the Council of Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius, the Persian church followed the Antiochene theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia and became the Church of the East (often called 'Nestorian' by opponents).
Chalcedon and the Oriental Orthodox

Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian churches rejected Chalcedon's 'in two natures' formula, preferring Cyril's 'one incarnate nature of God the Word'. Called 'Monophysite' by opponents, they describe themselves as Miaphysite; modern dialogues have found much common ground with Chalcedonians.
India: the Thomas Christians

Christians of Kerala trace their church to the apostle Thomas. Their presence is attested by the 6th century (Cosmas Indicopleustes), and they long received bishops from the Church of the East. After Portuguese pressure (Synod of Diamper, 1599) they divided into several churches, including the Malankara Orthodox.
China: Alopen and the Xi'an stele

A Church of the East mission led by Alopen reached the Tang capital Chang'an in 635 and received imperial permission to build a monastery. The Xi'an stele (781) recounts its history in Chinese and Syriac, presenting Christianity as the 'Luminous Teaching'.
Under Islam and the Mongols

After the Arab conquests (from 634) Christians in the Middle East became protected but subordinate communities, yet the Church of the East reached its greatest extent, from Mesopotamia to China, by the 13th century; the monk Rabban Sauma travelled from Beijing to Rome and Paris in 1287. The Mongol khanates' turn to Islam and the campaigns of Timur (c. 1400) devastated these churches.
New waves and today's global South

Catholic missions (Francis Xavier in Japan, 1549; Matteo Ricci in China from 1583) and later Protestant missions began a second wave in Asia and Africa. In the 20th century independent African churches, the East African Revival and Chinese house churches made Africa and Asia central to world Christianity.
paths/christianity-beyond-the-west/quiz/: Which kingdom is traditionally regarded as the first to adopt Christianity as its state religion?
Armenia under Tiridates III, traditionally dated 301 (some scholars prefer c. 314).
Who consecrated Frumentius as bishop for Aksum?
Athanasius, Patriarch of Alexandria, beginning Ethiopia's long link with the Coptic church.
The Xi'an stele, erected in 781, records the arrival of which missionary in 635?
Alopen led the Church of the East mission to the Tang capital Chang'an.
After which council did the Persian church become the separate Church of the East?
Ephesus' condemnation of Nestorius was not accepted by the Persian church, which followed Antiochene theology.
How do the Oriental Orthodox churches usually describe their Christology?
They call themselves Miaphysite ('one nature' of the incarnate Word, following Cyril); 'Monophysite' was a label used by opponents.
Indian Christians of Kerala trace their origin to which apostle?
The 'Thomas Christians' hold that the apostle Thomas evangelised South India.
Which Syriac poet-theologian wrote much of his theology as hymns?
Ephrem (d. 373), deacon of Nisibis and Edessa, is the great Syriac hymn-writer.
Which 14th-15th century development devastated the Church of the East across Asia?
The Mongol khanates' conversion to Islam and Timur's campaigns
Islamisation of the Mongol successor states and Timur's wars (c. 1400) destroyed much of the church's Asian network.
